title: Defined-lane 64-bit casts, and packed INT4 both ways
surface: cast(dst, src, CastConfig(round_mode=, saturate=, reg_layout=RegLayout.ZERO), mask); Reg(DT.int4) with reinterpret(DT.uint8) and pack4(); ub_to_reg_unpack4; reg_to_ub_normal through a MaskType.LOWEST32 mask
study_for: A single-register 64-bit cast defines half of what you might expect. Widening i32 to i64 doubles the bytes per lane, so one destination register holds 32 lanes and source lanes 32..63 have nowhere to go; narrowing i64 to i32 fills only the first 32 destination lanes for the same reason. Both stores go through a `MaskType.LOWEST32` mask, which is what stops the second source register -- undefined here -- from being read. Publishing the full 64 lanes would produce plausible garbage in the upper half rather than an error.

The argument-free i64-to-i32 narrowing ignores CTRL. It discards high bits whatever the saturation flags say (D-233), which makes it a different operation from a saturating narrowing rather than a special case of one. The inputs include +/-268435472 so the discarded word is visible in the result.

`i64` to `f32` rounds toward zero, and stating that took work on the reference side. Torch's own conversion rounds to nearest, so the reference computes the nearest result and then steps it back toward zero with `nextafter` when its magnitude overshot the integer. Without that, the reference would disagree with the kernel on exactly the values past FP32's exact range -- which is where the inputs are.

INT4 packs four nibbles to a byte with the low nibble carrying the even lane. `pack4()` on a `uint8` reinterpretation of an int4 register produces the dense carriers; `ub_to_reg_unpack4` reverses it, spreading 64 dense bytes into one byte in every four. The `i4_widen` carriers include 0x8F and 0x70 -- a negative nibble beside a positive one in the same byte -- so a widening that read the nibbles in the wrong order disagrees everywhere rather than subtly.

The reference never routes an integer through floating point. It packs signed nibbles directly with `clamp(-8, 7) & 15`, and narrows with Python-level ties-to-even, so the reference's own rounding is not borrowing the behaviour it is supposed to be checking.
do_not_copy_when: You need all 64 lanes of a 64-bit cast. That needs two destination registers and a second store; the forms here define 32, and the mask on the store is what keeps the promise honest.

Your values are not finite, or your conversion can overflow. The declared domain is finite values with int64 magnitudes below 2^40 and float-to-int64 inputs strictly inside the type. NaN handling and overflow are not claimed here -- `cast_saturation` is where the boundary behaviour is checked.
Your INT4 range is not [-8, 7]. The saturating narrowings clamp there, and an unsigned or offset nibble encoding is a different packing with a different reference.
You are assuming the narrowing respects your saturation setting. The argument-free i64-to-i32 form does not, on purpose. A saturating narrowing is a different call.
